assessment_summary:
1. Let G be a finite simple undirected unweighted graph, and let (A, B) be a partition of V(G) that cannot be improved by moving a single vertex. (Justified: Sets up the graph and the premise.)
2. Let C(A, B) denote the cut value, which is the number of edges with one endpoint in A and the other in B. (Justified: Definition of cut value.)
3. By the given premise, for any vertex v in A, the partition obtained by moving v to B has a cut value C(A \setminus \{v\}, B \cup \{v\}) \le C(A, B). (Justified: Follows from the assumption that the cut cannot be strictly improved.)
4. Similarly, for any vertex u in B, moving u to A yields a cut value C(A \cup \{u\}, B \setminus \{u\}) \le C(A, B). (Justified: Follows from the assumption that the cut cannot be strictly improved.)
5. Any arbitrary partition (A', B') of V(G) can be formed from (A, B) by choosing a subset of vertices X \subseteq A to move to B, and a subset of vertices Y \subseteq B to move to A. (Justified: Any partition can be reached by identifying which vertices need to change sides.)
6. The total change in the cut value when transforming (A, B) to (A', B') is exactly equal to the sum of the individual changes in the cut value caused by moving each vertex in X and Y independently. (Objection: False. The cut value function is not linear; moving two adjacent vertices simultaneously changes the cut value differently than the sum of their individual changes.)
7. Since moving any individual vertex in X or Y does not strictly increase the cut value (each individual change is \le 0), the sum of these individual changes must also be \le 0. (Objection: Relies on the flawed assumption of linearity in step 6.)
8. Therefore, the cut value C(A', B') is at most C(A, B). (Objection: Relies on flawed step 7.)
9. Because (A', B') was chosen as any arbitrary partition, no partition can have a strictly greater cut value than (A, B). (Objection: Relies on flawed step 8.)
10. Thus, (A, B) is a maximum cut. (Objection: Relies on flawed step 9.)
